entities.name: Alonso Sánchez
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alonso Sánchez de Huelva, an enigmatic figure of the early 15th century, is primarily remembered not for confirmed voyages but for an enduring, though largely unsubstantiated, legend that places him as a pre-Columbian discoverer of lands across the Atlantic. Born in Huelva, Spain, on the Atlantic coast of Andalusia around 1401, Sánchez was purportedly a mariner and merchant whose fateful westward journey, possibly driven by a storm, allegedly led him to what would later be known as the Americas. This narrative, circulating in various forms from the late 16th century onward, posits Sánchez as a direct antecedent to Christopher Columbus, influencing the larger discourse on the "discovery" of the New World and challenging the singular heroism often attributed to Columbus.

According to the most prevalent accounts, particularly those popularized by Inca Garcilaso de la Vega in his 1609 *Comentarios Reales de los Incas*, Sánchez embarked from Huelva, likely sometime between 1484 and 1492, sailing a small caravel or merchant vessel. A violent tempest, possibly a hurricane, is said to have driven his ship far off course into the uncharted western ocean. After weeks adrift, he supposedly sighted land, spent some time there, and then, with many of his crew dead from privation, managed to navigate back to the Atlantic islands, specifically Porto Santo in the Madeira archipelago. There, critically ill, he allegedly relayed his incredible tale and shared detailed charts and navigational data with a young Christopher Columbus, who was then residing on the island.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: While an alleged figure, Alonso Sánchez's legend significantly shaped the historical narrative of the "discovery" of the Americas, influencing how later generations perceived Columbus's originality and pre-Columbian contact. His story became a persistent counter-narrative within Iberian and broader European historiography.
